title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
hook: night three closes the clearing nights: the gods are offered a boon, and ask for something you can use again

segments.voice: Yesterday was night two of Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum: Durga, hard to pass, and the boat across. Did you choose a wall or a boat? Tonight, night three. Day one thousand one hundred eleven.

Choose a boon. The path heard the goddess say it to the gods earlier this year, reading the Devi Mahatmya whole. The buffalo demon is dead, the praise is sung, and the gods could ask for anything: riches, safety forever, a share of her power. Tonight is night three of Navaratri, the last of the clearing nights that, in one way of counting, belong to Durga. And that old request, from the end of the fourth chapter, comes back with a new job. Read inside a nine-night course, it turns out to be a lesson about coming back. Tonight, the boon again, as the close of the first stretch.
screen: `CHOOSE A BOON.` → `HEARD BEFORE.` → `NOW, A LESSON ABOUT COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's their answer, in paraphrase. Everything has already been done for us, they say, because our enemy is dead. But if you'll give us a boon, then whenever we remember you again, destroy our worst troubles. And for anyone who praises you with these hymns, be gracious to them too. The goddess agrees, and vanishes. Look at what they didn't ask for. Not a fortress that would last forever. Not a guarantee that nothing bad would happen again. As if they know it will. Heaven has been lost once; it can be lost twice. So they ask for something you can use again. Not a single rescue, but a promise of return: remember me, and I'll come. That's what makes this the right close for the first stretch of the curriculum. Clearing isn't a chore done once and crossed off a list. The road fills up again. Clutter comes back, worries come back, the same old anger comes back. What the first nights teach is not a final cleanup but a way of returning, the habit of remembering the one who clears. Some devotees take the line very literally: in trouble, they recite these chapters, or simply say the goddess's name. Others read it inwardly. The remembering is itself the clearing, the moment a person stops and turns toward something larger than the mess in front of them. And it widens the circle. The gods don't ask only for themselves. They ask for anyone who sings these hymns. Three nights in, the curriculum's first lesson is learned: what clears the road once can be called on again.
screen: `OUR ENEMY IS ALREADY DEAD.` · `WHENEVER WE REMEMBER YOU, COME.` · `NOT ONE RESCUE, A WAY OF RETURN.` · `FOR ANYONE WHO SINGS THESE HYMNS.` · then, large: `WHAT CLEARS THE ROAD CAN BE CALLED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: clearing, and remembering. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one thing that has crowded your road these three nights: a worry, a task, a grudge. Look at it, and on an out-breath, let it be set to one side, just for now. Notice the little room it leaves. Then think of what you'd turn to the next time it comes back: a name, a line, a person, a breath like this one. Rest there. If you pray, you can say the goddess's name, or the name you use, once, as the remembering. If you don't, let the breath be what you return to. The bell holds the time.
Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Night three closes the clearing nights, with the gods' boon: whenever we remember you, come. Today's word.
Your line: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Today, clear one thing out of the way, and choose what you'll return to when it piles up again. Day one thousand one hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Some devotees recite chapters of the Devi Mahatmya during Navaratri, or in times of trouble, holding to the gods' boon in chapter four that the goddess will come when she is remembered.

pairs: the goddess's offer to the gods

myth: the gods ask the goddess for riches and lasting safety
they ask that she come whenever they remember her, and destroy their worst troubles.
the gods ask the boon for others too
for anyone who praises her with these hymns.
the clearing nights promise a road that stays clear for good
the road fills up again; what the first nights teach is a way of returning.

fork.setup: it's night three, and the clearing nights are ending. the road will fill up again. what does the gods' boon suggest you carry into the next nights?
options: a promise that nothing will block the road again.
a way of returning: something to remember when it fills up.
a plan to stop clearing altogether.
fork.reveal: the gods don't ask for a road that stays clear. they ask that whenever they remember her, she destroy their worst troubles: a way of returning.

original.note: Sanskrit vara: a boon, a gift chosen by the one who receives it.

trapdoor: what you thought: once the demon is dead, the story is done.
what it means: the gods ask for a promise of return, so the clearing can happen again whenever it's needed.
what a scholar hears: Devi Mahatmya 4, the closing verses: the vara is not a possession but a promise of return, and then she vanishes from sight.

sources.ref: Devi Mahatmya 4 (closing verses: the boon asked by the gods)

notes: Devi Mahatmya 4 end (c. 4.33–4.39) paraphrased: the goddess offers a boon; the gods say all is done since their enemy is slain, but ask that whenever they remember her she destroy their worst calamities, and that she favor anyone who praises her with these hymns; she agrees and vanishes. 'Heaven has been lost once' refers to Mahishasura driving the gods from heaven (Devi Mahatmya 2); confirm.
Night three = close of Durga's stretch, agreed with the 1112 writer, whose review asks 'what did you clear out of the way?'. The carry sets that up.
Two readings (literal recitation in trouble; remembering as itself the clearing) attributed without ranking. Confirm.
